abstract: Galdin and Silbert (Dartmouth/Tuck and Princeton) study how LLMs disrupted labor market signaling on Freelancer.com, analyzing 2.7 million job applications across 61,000 postings in the coding/programming category. The paper documents that employer willingness to pay (WTP) for a one-standard-deviation increase in worker quality signals (credentials, experience, portfolio) fell from $25.67 to $14.85 after LLMs became available — a 42% decline. This signal degradation occurs because LLMs enable lower-quality workers to produce application materials that mimic high-quality workers, making traditional signals less informative. The authors model a counterfactual no-signaling equilibrium and estimate: a 5% average wage decline, 1.5% reduction in hiring, 4% loss of worker surplus, top-quintile workers hired 19% less often, and bottom-quintile workers hired 14% more often — suggesting LLMs compress the quality distribution visible to employers. Post-LLM, 14% of applications showed evidence of AI writing tool usage. The study provides one of the first empirical demonstrations of how LLMs can erode the informational infrastructure of labor markets, with implications extending well beyond freelance platforms.
keyFindings: Employer willingness to pay for a 1-SD increase in worker quality signals fell from $25.67 to $14.85 (42% decline) after LLMs became available on Freelancer.com coding jobs.
Counterfactual no-signaling equilibrium estimates: 5% average wage decline, 1.5% hiring reduction, and 4% worker surplus loss.
Top-quintile workers would be hired 19% less often and bottom-quintile workers 14% more often in a no-signaling equilibrium, indicating quality signal compression.
14% of post-LLM job applications showed evidence of AI writing tool usage, reflecting rapid adoption of LLMs for application preparation.
LLMs degrade labor market signaling by enabling lower-quality workers to produce application materials that mimic high-quality workers, reducing the information content of traditional credentials.
methodology: Empirical analysis of 2.7 million job applications across 61,000 postings on Freelancer.com in the coding/programming category, comparing pre- and post-LLM periods. The study estimates employer willingness to pay using revealed preference from hiring decisions and wage offers. A structural model of labor market signaling is used to compute counterfactual equilibrium outcomes under degraded signaling. AI writing tool usage detected through statistical analysis of application text features. The paper is a job market paper (Silbert JMP), indicating it has undergone faculty review but may not yet be peer-published.
qualifiers: Freelancer.com is a specific type of labor market (online freelancing for coding tasks) that may not generalize to traditional employment markets with interviews, references, and longer evaluation processes. The counterfactual no-signaling equilibrium is a modeled scenario, not an observed outcome. The 42% WTP decline may reflect platform-specific dynamics (race to the bottom on pricing, changing employer composition) beyond pure signaling degradation. The paper is a job market paper and has not yet undergone formal peer review. The 14% AI-assisted application rate was measured at a specific time and is likely higher now. Results may differ across occupational categories beyond coding.
